title: Understanding Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) and SPACs
content:
An Initial Public Offering (IPO) is the process by which a privately held corporation offers shares of its stock to the public on an exchange for the first time. Going public enables companies to raise capital from institutional and retail investors, provide liquidity to early employees and founders, and increase their public visibility.

The IPO process begins when a company hires investment banks to serve as underwriters. Underwriters assist with regulatory filings—chiefly the SEC Form S-1 prospectus—gauge investor appetite on 'roadshows,' and establish the initial public offering price. When trading commences, retail investors can purchase shares directly on the open market.

However, historical data shows that investing in newly public IPOs carries elevated volatility and risk. New issues frequently experience a first-day 'pop' driven by marketing hype, only to suffer prolonged price declines in subsequent quarters. A critical factor is the Lock-Up Expiration, usually 90 to 180 days after the IPO. During the lock-up period, insiders and early venture capital backers are legally prohibited from selling shares. When the lockup expires, insider selling often creates downward pressure on the stock.

An alternative path that gained prominence is the Special Purpose Acquisition Company (SPAC), often called a 'blank-check company.' A SPAC raises capital in an initial public offering with the sole intent of acquiring a private operating business. Because IPOs and SPACs involve unproven public track records, beginner investors are generally wise to wait several quarters until the company demonstrates consistent public earnings.
